motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of learning unnormalized statistical models in the presence of missing data, a common issue in real-world applications. Traditional methods for learning unnormalized models often rely on score matching, which involves estimating the score function of the data distribution. However, these methods face several practical challenges, including the need for an auxiliary network to estimate the score function, the requirement for the model to support sampling, and the difficulty in estimating the score function for high-dimensional data. These limitations can lead to suboptimal performance and computational inefficiency. To overcome these issues, the paper proposes a new approach that leverages adversarial learning to estimate model parameters without the need for an auxiliary network. The proposed method, Adversarial Score Matching (ASM), aims to maximize the score discrepancy between the data distribution and the model distribution, thereby achieving consistent and efficient parameter estimation. The paper also introduces a method to handle missing data, which is a common and challenging scenario in many real-world applications. By addressing these limitations, the proposed approach aims to provide a more practical and efficient solution for learning unnormalized models with missing data.
idea: The paper introduces Adversarial Score Matching (ASM), a novel method for learning unnormalized statistical models in the presence of missing data. ASM estimates model parameters by maximizing the score discrepancy between the data distribution and the model distribution, without the need for an auxiliary network. The method involves a proximal gradient algorithm that iteratively updates the model parameters by maximizing the score discrepancy. The paper also proposes a multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) estimator for the score discrepancy, which is computationally more efficient than the traditional importance sampling estimator. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that ASM can be interpreted as an adversarial learning algorithm, providing a deeper understanding of its behavior and effectiveness. The proposed methods are validated through extensive experiments on various unnormalized models and missing data mechanisms, showing improved performance and computational efficiency compared to existing score matching methods.
title: Learning Unnormalized Models with Missing Data via Adversarial Score Matching
abstract: Learning unnormalized model parameters is a challenging task that frequently arises in various scientific fields. Score matching is a promising method to learn unnormalized models by estimating the score function. However, score matching has several practical challenges in real-world applications, including the need for an auxiliary network to estimate the score function, the requirement for the model to support sampling, and the difficulty of estimating the score function for high-dimensional data. To address these challenges, we propose adversarial score matching (ASM), an adversarial learning algorithm for learning unnormalized models, which does not require an auxiliary network and can be applied to high-dimensional data. We also propose a multilevel Monte Carlo estimator for the score discrepancy, which is computationally more efficient than the traditional importance sampling estimator. In addition, we demonstrate that ASM is a mode-seeking algorithm, which has been observed empirically in a variety of adversarial learning methods. We evaluate the performance of ASM on various unnormalized models and missing data mechanisms, and demonstrate that ASM outperforms existing score matching methods.

Experimental_Setup.name: Simple Energy-Based Models
Experimental_Setup.description: This experiment evaluates the performance of ASM and MissDiff on simple energy-based models with missing data. The purpose is to compare the sample quality and imputation performance of ASM with existing methods. The experiment uses a toy example where three energy-based models are trained on a mixture of Gaussians with 5 modes. The dataset consists of 5,000 samples, and 50% of the dimensions are masked using one hot masking. The models are based on a multi-layer perceptron and approximate the score function using denoising diffusion probabilistic models. The energy function is evaluated on the test samples, and the mean energy is computed with 1000 samples. The experiment is repeated 5 times with different random seeds.

Experimental_Setup.name: Gaussian Graphical Models
Experimental_Setup.description: This experiment assesses the performance of ASM and MissDiff on Gaussian graphical models with missing data. The goal is to evaluate the models' ability to capture the data distribution in the presence of missing data. The experiment uses a dataset where 25% of the dimensions are masked using one hot masking. The graphical structure is sampled from the hyper-geometric distribution. The models are fitted using the trimmed graphical loss with a Gaussian noise level of 0.3. The sample quality and imputation performance are measured using the energy function, KL divergence, and Wasserstein-2 distance. The energy function is evaluated on the test samples, and the KL divergence and Wasserstein-2 distance are computed using the energy functions learned from the training samples. The experiment is repeated 5 times with different random seeds.

Experimental_Setup.name: Spliced Gene Expression Data
Experimental_Setup.description: This experiment evaluates the performance of ASM and MissDiff on real-world spliced gene expression data from yeast cells. The purpose is to assess the models' ability to capture complex, real-world data distributions with missing data. The dataset consists of 250,000 genes labeled with 22 different transcription factors. 25% of the genes are masked out for training, and the masked-out genes are used only for testing. The dense layer in the score network takes the masked values as 0. The models are compared using the mean and standard deviation of the energy function on the test samples. The energy function is evaluated using the imputed values. The experiment is repeated 5 times with different random seeds.
